name: Heavy Metal
blurb: From a Birmingham factory floor to stadium thunder, the loud history of metal.

questions.prompt: Which Birmingham band recorded "Paranoid" in 1970?
questions.fact: The song was written and recorded in minutes to fill out the album, and it became the band's biggest hit.

questions.fact: Halford helped make black leather and studs the standard look for metal, and he came out publicly in 1998.

questions.fact: He made himself plastic fingertips from a melted bottle and tuned his guitar down to ease the strain, and the heavier sound became Sabbath's trademark.

questions.prompt: Where did Iron Maiden's name come from?
questions.fact: Bassist Steve Harris has said he took the name after seeing the film The Man in the Iron Mask.

questions.prompt: Which band, led by bassist Lemmy, recorded "Ace of Spades" in 1980?
questions.fact: Lemmy's growling vocals and distorted Rickenbacker bass drove the song, and Lemmy, a devoted gambler, treated the lyric as a card game.

stories.title: Black Sabbath, Recorded in a Day
stories.dek: Four Birmingham lads and a very loud first album
stories.body:
Aston is a working-class district of Birmingham, England, and in the late 1960s it was a place of factories and rows of terraced houses. Four young men from the area, singer Ozzy Osbourne, guitarist Tony Iommi, bassist Geezer Butler and drummer Bill Ward, formed a blues band called Earth. They played local clubs, and they were not sure they were any good.

Then Iommi had an accident. On his last day in a sheet-metal factory, a machine crushed the tips of two fingers on his right hand. Doctors feared he would never play again. Instead, he made himself fingertip caps out of a melted plastic bottle, loosened the strings of his guitar to ease the strain, and carried on. The lower, thicker sound he got would help define the band.

The group changed its name after noticing that people lined up in cinemas to be scared. They borrowed the title of a 1963 Boris Karloff horror film, Black Sabbath, and Butler began writing lyrics about dark subjects. Their song "Black Sabbath" opened with a slow, tolling riff built on a tritone, an interval that centuries earlier had been called the devil's interval.

In October 1969 they went into Regent Sound studio in London with producer Rodger Bain. They had very little money and almost no time. The band played its live set straight through, with Ozzy singing over the top, and the whole album was recorded in about a day, then mixed the next. A tolling bell, rain and thunder open the first track.

The album, Black Sabbath, was released on Friday, February 13, 1970. Critics were unkind, but the public was fascinated. It reached No. 8 in the UK and the top 25 in the US. Later that year the band followed it with Paranoid, whose title song was thrown together at the last minute when the label wanted a single. "Paranoid" became a UK Top 5 hit, and the album went to No. 1.

Sabbath created a template that bands still follow. They tuned down, slowed down and wrote about war, madness and fear, not love. Critics eventually came around, and later bands including Metallica, Judas Priest and Iron Maiden cited them as an inspiration. Osbourne, Iommi, Butler and Ward would go on to sell millions of records, but nothing sounds quite like the first record made in a single day by four young men with nothing to lose.

stories.title: Fire on Lake Geneva
stories.dek: How a burning casino became the most famous riff in rock
stories.body:
In December 1971 Deep Purple arrived in Montreux, Switzerland, to make a new album. The plan was to record in the town's Casino, a large entertainment complex on the shore of Lake Geneva, using the Rolling Stones' mobile recording studio, a truck packed with equipment. The band was at the peak of its powers, and singer Ian Gillan, guitarist Ritchie Blackmore, bassist Roger Glover, keyboardist Jon Lord and drummer Ian Paice wanted to work somewhere quiet and distant from London.

On the night of December 4, they went to the casino to watch Frank Zappa and the Mothers of Invention play. Partway through the show, a fan in the audience fired a flare gun at the ceiling. The decorations were made of rattan, and they went up at once. The crowd streamed out into the cold, and the casino was destroyed. Montreux Jazz Festival founder Claude Nobs, whom the band knew, helped get people out of the building.

The band stood on the shore and watched the smoke drift across the lake. Their recording plans were ruined, since the casino was gone. After a few false starts, they rented the Grand Hotel, which was empty for the season, and set up the mobile studio in the hallway. They played in the corridors, and the band sometimes had to stop when the neighbors complained about the noise.

Blackmore came up with a simple riff, played on two strings in fourths, and the band built a song around it. Glover suggested the title, and Gillan wrote the lyrics as a news report of everything that had happened. The lyric tells the story of the night in plain terms, from the trip to Montreux to the smoke over the lake, and gives a nod to Claude Nobs for his part in the rescue.

The album, Machine Head, came out in 1972. The song was not planned as a single, and the band did not think it was single material. But when it was released as a single in the US in 1973, it reached No. 4. The riff became the first thing many young guitarists learned to play. Today a statue of Freddie Mercury stands by the lake in Montreux, and the town still hosts a famous festival. The fire that destroyed the casino also gave metal one of its best-loved songs.

stories.title: Master of Puppets and the Road to Sweden
stories.dek: A thrash classic and the loss of Cliff Burton
stories.body:
By 1986 Metallica was the leading band of a new kind of heavy metal, called thrash, which was faster and angrier than what came before. The band had formed in Los Angeles in 1981 and moved to the San Francisco Bay Area, where it found a loyal following. Their first two albums, Kill 'Em All and Ride the Lightning, had sold steadily by word of mouth. For the third, they traveled to Copenhagen, Denmark, to work with producer Flemming Rasmussen at Sweet Silence Studios.

The album, Master of Puppets, was recorded in the fall of 1985. Its title song, which runs more than eight minutes, tells of addiction and control, and its guitar work is quick, precise and complex. Bassist Cliff Burton, who had studied classical music, contributed to the song's harmonies and wrote the melodic passage in the middle section. Singer James Hetfield and drummer Lars Ulrich pushed the band toward bigger and more ambitious arrangements, and guitarist Kirk Hammett added solos that fans would memorize.

Released in March 1986, the album reached the Billboard Top 30 with almost no radio play, and it later went multi-platinum. Many critics now call it one of the greatest metal albums ever made, and in 2016 the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry.

In 1986 Metallica toured the US as the opening act for Ozzy Osbourne's band, and then went to Europe in the autumn, with a run of dates in Scandinavia. On the night of September 26, 1986, the band's bus was driving through southern Sweden on a cold, wet road. According to the band, the members had drawn cards for the bunks, and Burton had won the choice of beds. At dawn on September 27 the bus skidded on ice near the town of Ljungby, and it rolled over. Burton was thrown from the bus and died. He was 24 years old.

The band considered breaking up. Hetfield, Ulrich and Hammett decided that Burton would have wanted them to continue, and they auditioned bassists, choosing Jason Newsted, who came from the band Flotsam and Jetsam. They went back on the road, and later releases, including the "Black Album" in 1991, made them one of the best-selling rock bands in the world.

Fans still remember Burton as a gifted musician, and his bass solos, especially "Anesthesia (Pulling Teeth)", remain a model for how heavy music can borrow from classical technique.

stories.title: Lemmy Plays Ace of Spades
stories.dek: A bassist who played chords, a gambler's song and a band named after a Hawkwind track.
stories.body:
Lemmy Kilmister had been fired from Hawkwind in 1975, after an arrest at the Canadian border, and he decided to start a band that played faster and louder than anything he had been in before. He named it Motörhead, after the last song he wrote for his old group. The band went through changes in its lineup, and by 1980 it had settled into a trio of Lemmy on bass and vocals, Eddie Clarke on guitar and Phil Taylor on drums.

Lemmy's bass playing was one of the group's trademarks. He played a Rickenbacker bass through guitar amplifiers, with the volume up and the tone distorted, and he often strummed chords where other bassists would play single notes. The result was a thick, grinding sound that fans said could fill a room. His voice was a raspy shout that sounded like a man who had spent a lot of nights in smoky rooms, and he sang about speed, gambling and life on the road.

Ace of Spades was recorded in 1980 with producer Vic Maile at Jackson's Studios in Hertfordshire. The song opens with a bass riff that builds quickly and never relents. Taylor's drumming is rapid-fire, and Clarke's guitar solo keeps the energy going. The title and the lyrics are about gambling, and Lemmy has said that he loved to gamble, especially on fruit machines in pubs and bars. The song uses the card game as a metaphor for living on the edge, and it is easy to hear that attitude in the music.

The record helped bridge the gap between heavy metal and punk. Metal fans appreciated the heavy riffs, and punks appreciated the speed and the lack of frills. For that reason the band was welcomed by both camps, and Motörhead became a respected name in both worlds. It also helped inspire the thrash bands that followed in the 1980s, including Metallica, who have often named Lemmy as an influence.

Lemmy kept playing until his death in December 2015, and he rarely changed his style. He wore black, played loud and told stories with a dry sense of humor. Ace of Spades stayed a favorite at his shows, and for many fans it is the song that defined him.

stories.title: Ozzy Starts Over
stories.dek: A fired singer, a young guitarist and a song about a crazy train.
stories.body:
In April 1979 Black Sabbath fired Ozzy Osbourne. The singer had been a founding member, and his departure left him with an uncertain future. He reportedly spent some weeks in a hotel room, feeling sorry for himself, until Sharon Arden, the daughter of music manager Don Arden, encouraged him to start again. She would later become his wife and his manager.

The new band needed a guitarist. Ozzy auditioned a young player from Los Angeles named Randy Rhoads, who had played with Quiet Riot. Rhoads had studied classical guitar, and his family ran a music school where he also taught. Ozzy has said that he hired Rhoads after a very short audition, once he heard the way Rhoads warmed up. Bassist Bob Daisley and drummer Lee Kerslake, both with experience in British rock, completed the lineup.

They recorded the album Blizzard of Ozz in England in 1980. Crazy Train was written by Osbourne, Rhoads and Daisley. The song begins with a bright, bouncing guitar riff that Rhoads came up with, and it has a steady stomp that suits the singer's voice. Daisley wrote most of the lyrics, and he has said they were about the fears of the Cold War and the possibility of nuclear disaster. The vocal melody and the explosive solo give the song its shape.

Rhoads brought a new sound to heavy metal. His classical training showed up in the careful way he built solos and in the neat melodic lines that run through the album. Fans noticed that he was not a typical hard rock guitarist, and many other guitarists took lessons from his playing. In just two albums he established himself as one of the major guitarists of his era.

The story took a sad turn on March 19, 1982, when Rhoads died in a plane crash in Florida while on tour. He was 25. Ozzy has said that he has missed his friend ever since, and Crazy Train still carries the memory of the partnership.

Blizzard of Ozz showed that a singer could survive losing his old band, if he found the right partner. It remains a landmark of the genre.

stories.title: Welcome to the Jungle
stories.dek: Guns N' Roses arrive from the Sunset Strip.
stories.body:
Guns N' Roses came together in Los Angeles in 1985 with Axl Rose on vocals, Slash and Izzy Stradlin on guitars, Duff McKagan on bass and Steven Adler on drums. The band played the clubs of the Sunset Strip and built a reputation for loud, dangerous shows. In 1986 they signed with Geffen Records, and the following year they released their first album, Appetite for Destruction.

Welcome to the Jungle opens the record. The first sound is a long, shimmering guitar figure that sets a mood of tension. Then the band comes in at full power, with a slashing riff and a thick, fast beat. Rose's voice shifts from a low growl to a high wail, and the lyrics describe the shock of arriving in a big city with no safety net. The album was produced by Mike Clink at Rumbo Recorders in the Los Angeles area.

The inspiration for the words reportedly came from a trip Rose took to New York City. He has said that someone on the street told him he was in the jungle and that he was going to be in trouble. The remark stuck with him and became the heart of the song. Rose was from Indiana, and he had come to Los Angeles looking for a way into music, so the theme felt personal.

The music video helped bring the band to a wider audience. It shows a young man arriving in the city by bus, with the band performing in a series of scenes and with television screens showing images of the streets. Rose's snaking dance became a hallmark of his stage style. The video was played on MTV, though it took some time before it became a regular fixture.

Appetite for Destruction did not take off right away. The record was released in July 1987, and the band spent months on the road, building a following one show at a time. The breakthrough came later, when Sweet Child O' Mine and other songs reached a wider audience, and the album went on to become a landmark of hard rock.

Welcome to the Jungle remains the band's calling card. In the first minute it tells you exactly what kind of band this is.

stories.title: Made in Japan
stories.dek: Deep Purple on tour in August 1972, tape rolling.
stories.body:
In the summer of 1972 Deep Purple was one of the loudest and busiest bands in the world. Their album Machine Head had come out earlier that year, and a tour took them to Japan in August. The lineup was the one fans consider the classic: Ian Gillan on vocals, Ritchie Blackmore on guitar, Jon Lord on keyboards, Roger Glover on bass and Ian Paice on drums.

The shows were recorded on August 15 and 16 at Festival Hall in Osaka and on August 17 at the Budokan in Tokyo. The label reportedly planned to release the live recording only in Japan, and the band was not especially keen on putting it out more widely. Roger Glover took part in mixing the tapes, and after listening to the results the group agreed that the material was strong enough to release around the world.

The double album that came out was called Made in Japan. It contained seven long tracks, including Highway Star, Child in Time, Smoke on the Water, Strange Kind of Woman and Space Truckin'. The performances are extended and full of improvisation, with the band stretching out songs well beyond their studio versions. Blackmore's guitar solos, Lord's organ runs and Gillan's piercing voice make for a record that sounds like a band at its peak.

Smoke on the Water had been released on Machine Head earlier that year, and the live version shows how much the song grew on stage. The famous four-note riff is played with a thick, steady beat, and the crowd's enthusiasm can be heard. Fans who bought the album often point to that track as the first one they learned on guitar.

The album has been called one of the great live records of its time, and it has influenced many hard rock and heavy metal bands. It also arrived at a turning point for Deep Purple. Within a year, tensions in the band led to the departure of Gillan and Glover, and the classic lineup came to an end.

Made in Japan gave the band a final document of that lineup at its best. It was recorded in a few nights, and it still holds up as an example of what a loud band can do live.

stories.title: Monsters of Rock in Moscow
stories.dek: A free show at an airfield, weeks after the coup.
stories.body:
On September 28, 1991, a huge crowd gathered at Tushino Airfield in Moscow for a free rock festival. The bill was AC/DC, Metallica, Pantera and the Black Crowes, along with a Soviet band called E.S.T. It was billed as Monsters of Rock, a name used for hard rock festivals in Europe, and it was the first time many of these bands had played in the Soviet Union.

The timing was striking. A failed coup attempt had shaken the country a little more than a month earlier, in August, and the Soviet Union was close to collapse. Just a few years earlier, rock music of this sort had been difficult to hear in the country. Now hundreds of thousands of people came out to hear it live, and estimates of the crowd have ranged from several hundred thousand to more than a million.

Metallica played a set that included Enter Sandman, which had been released only a few weeks earlier on the Black Album. The song's heavy, slow groove and its dark theme suited the huge outdoor stage. The band was at the height of its popularity, and the festival gave it a chance to reach fans who had never heard it in person. AC/DC closed the show, with Angus Young in his schoolboy outfit, running along the stage.

The concert was filmed and released as a documentary, and the footage shows a sea of people stretching across the field, with banners and flags. The crowd looks young and excited, and many are wearing homemade shirts. Musicians who were there have often said it was one of the most memorable shows they ever played.

For fans in the Soviet Union, the day was a milestone. It was a chance to see big Western bands in person, and to be part of a crowd that was celebrating a new era. Within a few months the Soviet Union would be dissolved, and the festival came to be remembered as a symbol of the change.

Monsters of Rock in Moscow shows how music can travel across borders and times. It was a loud day at an airfield, and it meant much more than that to the people who were there.

covers.title: Cum On Feel the Noize
covers.note: Noddy Holder and Jim Lea wrote it, and Slade had a UK number one in 1973. Quiet Riot's version helped send Metal Health to number one on the US album chart.

covers.title: Turn the Page
covers.note: Seger released it on Back in '72 in 1973 and again in a live version in 1976. Metallica's darker take appeared on Garage Inc.

covers.title: Am I Evil?
covers.note: Diamond Head released it on their 1980 debut Lightning to the Nations. Metallica recorded it in 1984 as a B side, and Lars Ulrich has called Diamond Head a major influence.

covers.title: Smokin' in the Boys Room
covers.note: The Michigan band Brownsville Station had a top five hit with it in 1973. Mötley Crüe's 1985 version reached the US top 20.

covers.title: You Really Got Me
covers.note: Ray Davies wrote it, and the Kinks had a UK number one in 1964. It follows the solo Eruption on Van Halen's debut and was the band's first single.

covers.title: Land of Confusion
covers.note: Genesis released it on Invisible Touch in 1986, with a video using Spitting Image puppets. Disturbed's 2005 version was a hard rock radio hit.

covers.title: Diamonds and Rust
covers.note: Baez wrote it, widely understood to be about Bob Dylan, and released it in 1975. Judas Priest recorded a heavy version for Sin After Sin.

covers.title: The Green Manalishi (With the Two-Pronged Crown)
covers.album: Hell Bent for Leather (Bonus Track Version)
covers.note: Peter Green reportedly wrote it after a nightmare, and Fleetwood Mac released it in 1970. Priest's studio version appeared on the US edition of Killing Machine, titled Hell Bent for Leather.
